(1) Those port and rail facilities in New Jersey originally included in the present New York Exempt Zone (generally east of Newark Bay and the Hackensack River).
(2) New Jersey port facilities which have been given the same area of exempt operations as points in the present New York Exempt Zone with respect to shipments having a prior or subsequent movement by water. Movements between these ports (Port Newark, 53 M.C.C. at 489-93, and Port Elizabeth, 84 M.C.C. 747) and points within the exempt zone of New York City are exempt from federal economic regulation.
(3) New Jersey rail facilities which have been given the same area of exempt operations as points in the present New York Exempt Zone with respect to shipments having a prior or subsequent movement by rail. These terminals are: Kearny, N.J., 88 M.C.C. 336, Lehigh Valley R.R. TOFC Terminal, 111 M.C.C. 123, Reading Railroad TOFC Terminal, 112 M.C.C. 203, and Central of N.J. TOFC Terminal, 113 M.C.C. 891.
These exemptions from our regulation have been accorded to these facilities in recognition of their integral relationship with New York City rail and shipping facilities. The New Jersey facilities are extensions of the older, smaller facilities in the city itself. Locating in New Jersey was dictated, in large measure, by the shortage of available land in New York City. Functionally, the New Jersey and New York facilities are interchangeable. For example, a shipment coming into the harbor is generally tagged as destined to the Port of New York, and whether it is unloaded at a pier in New York City or on the New Jersey
The freight forwarders have also submitted evidence concerning the establishment of satellite terminals in New York City suburbs due to the problems of land shortages and rising costs and the need for modern facilities. They propose a uniform terminal area including all points within 20 miles of the New York City corporate limits for forwarder or carriers serving points in New York City commercial zone.
